messages.content: You used to repair roofs, didn't you? Do you ever miss the people you worked beside?
I do miss the smell of tar and hot oil on a Tuesday afternoon, but I miss the people more.
It sounds quiet now, just the wind above us.
The valley wind is different; it carries the smell of dogs and frying fat, not stone dust.
Were you happy fixing those leaky tiles?
I was tired, mostly, but yes, I was happy when someone finally walked in without dripping on their shoes.
Your teacher, Mara, must have been a good one.
She was good at explaining why the rafters needed support, not just how to drive in the nails.
Do you talk to her often?
Sometimes, when the hammer hits the nail and the sound is too sharp, I tell her to stop hitting so hard.
She sounds like she's watching.
She's not watching; she's just in the corner of the room with a cup of tea that's gone cold.
That's a gentle way to put it.
It is, because I don't need to keep her alive for the rest of my days.
So you're just... alone?
I'm alone with a roof that needs shingles and a body that aches in the morning.
Does that feel like freedom or just isolation?
I think it's just a trade-off; I have the quiet, but I lost the crowd to laugh with at noon.
Did you ever feel trapped by the mountain?
Not trapped, exactly, but heavy sometimes, like the roof is too thick for my back to carry.
You seem to carry a lot of weight, even now.
I carry the memory of how to patch a hole, and the weight of knowing I chose this path myself.
That's a lot to remember.
It is, but I remember the specific weight of a nail, not the general concept of suffering.
Is there anything you'd change about those roof jobs?
I'd change the rain, because even when the work was perfect, the rain never stopped complaining.
So the rain was the real problem?
The rain was just the weather; the real problem was how we couldn't stop it from leaking into our socks.
That's a practical complaint.
It is, because nobody likes to walk through mud when they're just trying to dry their boots.
I imagine the view from up there must be different.
The view is just the view, but the air up there is thin and makes my chest feel like it's holding a full bag of bricks.
You're still in the valley, aren't you?
I live just below the summit, near where the path forks and people walk toward the fields.
Does anyone visit you often?
A few neighbors come up once a month to borrow a hammer, but mostly I'm just a house with a door.
That sounds lonely, even if you enjoy the work.
It is lonely, but not the kind that makes you want to scream; it's the kind that makes you listen to the silence.
What do you listen to when it's quiet?
I listen to the wind trying to get under the shingles and the way the leaves scratch against the wood.
That's peaceful.
It is, until I remember I'm still a human with a temper and a back that aches after a long day.
I hope you find some peace in that.
I hope I find enough peace to fix the roof without breaking the tile; the rest is just luck.
Good luck with the next repair.
Thanks, and go enjoy your own day before the rain comes down.
